note.note:
History & Physical (Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
46-year-old right-handed woman with 2-week progressive numbness and weakness of the left upper limb (elbow→hand, palmar digits 2–4) and a prior 20-minute episode of left-eye visual-field loss; clinician concerned for possible demyelinating process and has arranged an urgent neurology referral for further investigation.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Progressive numbness, tingling, and subjective weakness in the left arm.  
• Onset & course: Began ≈2 weeks ago after starting a boxing class; initially mild tingling, now constant numbness extending from elbow to hand. Symptoms worsening.  
• Distribution: Palmar aspect of 2nd, 3rd, and 4th fingers; occasional shoulder discomfort with movement; no significant neck pain.  
• Functional impact: Difficulty striking piano keys; occasional object-dropping; weakness perceived as sensory-related rather than pain-limited.  
• Provoking/relieving measures: Massage, warm baths, ibuprofen—no relief.  
• Associated symptoms: One episode of transient (≈20 min) partial visual loss in left eye a few weeks ago; occasional “tired headaches” and generalized fatigue; no seizures, no lower-limb involvement, gait normal.  
• Recent illnesses: Severe “cold/flu” one month ago lasting ≈2 weeks.  
• ROS (pertinent negatives/positives): No neck pain, no seizures/fits, no dizziness, no speech disturbance, no facial droop, no bowel/bladder symptoms reported.

Past Medical History:
• Generally healthy; no chronic diagnoses reported.  
• Recent viral upper-respiratory illness (self-limited).  
Medications:
  – Ibuprofen PRN for musculoskeletal pain (dose/route/frequency not documented)  
  – Vitamin D supplement (dose/route/frequency not documented)  
  – Iron supplement occasionally (dose/route/frequency not documented)  
  – Melatonin occasionally for sleep (dose/route/frequency not documented)  
Allergies: Not documented.

Social History:
• Occupation not specified; notes working long hours.  
• Physically active; recently began boxing classes.  
• Alcohol: Occasional binge—recent episode of heavy drinking at a work celebration.  
• Tobacco & recreational drugs: Not mentioned.  
• Hobbies: Plays piano.  
• Lives in secure location (per tele-consult); other social factors not discussed.

Family History:
• Father – hypothyroidism and unspecified autoimmune condition.  
• Mother – type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia.  
• No known family neurological disorders.

Physical Examination:
(Not performed during video consult; no vitals recorded.)

Investigations:
None to date.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Left upper-limb numbness/weakness  
  • Differential includes cervical radiculopathy, median nerve entrapment, and demyelinating disease (e.g., multiple sclerosis).  
  • Plan: Urgent neurology referral for comprehensive neurological examination and MRI brain/spine ± nerve conduction studies. Advise patient to monitor for progression (leg weakness, balance issues, worsening sensory loss) and present to Emergency Department if these occur.

Issue 2 – Transient left-eye visual field loss  
  • Could represent optic neuritis (demyelinating) or vascular event.  
  • Plan: Included in neurology referral; consider MRI with optic nerve sequences and formal ophthalmologic assessment if suggested by neurology.

Issue 3 – Possible musculoskeletal/nerve compression related to boxing  
  • Less likely primary cause but may contribute to symptoms.  
  • Plan: Relative rest from high-impact boxing pending neurologic evaluation; continue conservative measures (NSAIDs PRN); reassess after specialist review.

General advice  
  • Return immediately for any new neurologic deficits, persistent visual loss, severe headache, vomiting, or seizures.  
  • No disease-specific medication initiated until diagnosis confirmed.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Cervical radiculopathy (likelihood: Moderate-High)  
   – Dermatomal-type numbness from elbow to palmar digits; onset after neck/shoulder exertion with boxing. Lack of neck pain is opposing but not exclusive.  
2. Median nerve entrapment (carpal tunnel/proximal median neuropathy) (likelihood: Moderate)  
   – Classic palmar 2–4 digit involvement and repetitive hand trauma; proximal arm symptoms less typical.  
3. Multiple sclerosis (likelihood: Moderate)  
   – Separate neurologic events (transient visual loss + evolving arm sensory deficit) in a 46-year-old woman; recent viral illness and family autoimmune history supportive, but brevity of visual episode less typical.

Quality checks:
● Missing/expected elements: Allergies not obtained; no vital signs; no formal neurological or musculoskeletal examination; no medication reconciliation with doses/frequencies; smoking status undocumented.  
● Transcript/DDx conflicts: Clinician emphasized MS; DDx ranks cervical radiculopathy slightly higher—no direct conflict, but differing emphasis noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; occasional interruptions but overall intelligible.
